name: MathlibAnnex.Mollification.mollify
title: Mollification by a normalized smooth kernel

content.display_title: Mollification by a normalized smooth kernel
content.one_sentence_role: Defines convolution with a nonnegative smooth kernel of integral one.
content.natural_language_statement: Let $X=\mathbb R^n$ and $Y=\mathbb R^N$, with their coordinate sup norms and Lebesgue measure on $X$. For a real parameter $\varepsilon$ and a map $f:X\to Y$, define $f_\varepsilon=\rho_\varepsilon*f$, where $\rho_\varepsilon$ is the normalized bump described below.
content.definition_explanation:
For $\varepsilon>0$, take the specified smooth bump $\varphi_\varepsilon$ centered at $0$, with inner radius $\varepsilon/2$ and outer radius $\varepsilon$. For $\varepsilon\leq0$, the definition instead uses radii $1/2$ and $1$. Set
$$\begin{aligned}
\rho_\varepsilon(y)&=\frac{\varphi_\varepsilon(y)}{\int_{\mathbb R^n}\varphi_\varepsilon(z)\,dz},\\
f_\varepsilon(x)&=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho_\varepsilon(y)f(x-y)\,dy.
\end{aligned}$$
The denominator is positive. This normalization followed by convolution is the complete definition. The fallback defines the operation at every real parameter; approximation uses only $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.
content.assumptions: The definition accepts every $n,N\geq0$, every real $\varepsilon$, and every function $f$. It does not assume continuity, measurability, or integrability. Analytic properties of the convolution require their own hypotheses.
content.conclusion: The output is the function $f_\varepsilon:X\to Y$. For locally integrable $f$ this is the ordinary convolution with the compactly supported continuous kernel. For arbitrary $f$ the displayed integral is understood with the source library's total Bochner-integral convention (zero when Bochner integrability fails).
content.lean_realization_notes:
For $\varepsilon>0$, the same normalized bump satisfies
$$\rho_\varepsilon\geq0,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho_\varepsilon(y)\,dy=1,\qquad
\rho_\varepsilon(y)=0\quad\text{if }\|y\|_\infty\geq\varepsilon.$$
In particular its topological support, $\overline{\{y:\rho_\varepsilon(y)\ne0\}}$, is contained in $\overline B_\infty(0,\varepsilon)$. The definition fixes these bumps; no formula identifying them as dilates of a single kernel is asserted. Smoothness of $f_\varepsilon$ and convergence are separate results.
